source_refs.note: PDF 262-264 (book p. 260-262): csc x domain and range, Figure 9.10, principal cosecant function, csc^-1 domain and range, Figures 9.11(a) and 9.11(b)

blocks.text: The graph of the function \(f(x) = \csc x\) with domain \(\{x \mid x \in \mathbb{R} \wedge x \ne n\pi,\ n \in \mathbb{Z}\}\) and range is the set \(\mathbb{R} - (-1, 1)\) is shown in Figure 9.10.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Where do this domain and range come from? \(\csc x = \frac{1}{\sin x}\). Division by zero is not allowed, so we remove every \(x\) where \(\sin x = 0\), that is \(x = n\pi\) (\(0, \pm\pi, \pm 2\pi, \dots\)). At these points the graph has vertical asymptotes (the dashed lines in Figure 9.10).
Since \(-1 \le \sin x \le 1\), the reciprocal always has size at least 1: \(|\csc x| \ge 1\). So \(\csc x\) never takes a value strictly between \(-1\) and \(1\). That is what \(\mathbb{R} - (-1, 1)\) means; written as intervals it is \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\).

blocks.alt: Graph of y = csc x for x from minus 2 pi to 2 pi. Dashed vertical asymptotes at x = minus 2 pi, minus pi, 0, pi and 2 pi. Dashed horizontal lines y = 1 and y = minus 1. U-shaped branches open upward with lowest points (minus 3 pi over 2, 1) and (pi over 2, 1); branches open downward with highest points (minus pi over 2, minus 1) and (3 pi over 2, minus 1). No part of the graph lies between y = minus 1 and y = 1.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.10: graph of \(y = \csc x\) from \(-2\pi\) to \(2\pi\) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: Clearly from the graph it follows that cosecant function is not bijective because the line \(y = 1\) and \(y = -1\) touches the graph at many points. However, if we restrict the domain of \(f(x) = \csc x\) to the interval \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right] - \{0\}\), then the function with restricted domain i.e. \(f : \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, 0\right) \cup \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) \(\to (-\infty, 1) \cup (1, \infty)\) becomes one-one and onto that is invertible and is called principal cosecant function. blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The book prints the codomain of the restricted function as \((-\infty, 1) \cup (1, \infty)\). That set wrongly contains every number between \(-1\) and \(1\) (which \(\csc x\) never takes) and leaves out \(-1\) and \(1\) (which it does take: \(\csc\frac{\pi}{2} = 1\), \(\csc\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = -1\)). The correct statement is
\[f : \left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right) \cup \left(0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\]
\[\to (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\]
which matches the book's own summary table in 9.1.6.

blocks.text_alt: y equals inverse cosecant of x if and only if x equals cosecant of y

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why this particular piece of the graph? On \(\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), \(\sin x\) increases from 0 to 1, so \(\csc x\) decreases from \(+\infty\) down to 1: every value \(\ge 1\) is taken exactly once. On \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, 0\right)\), \(\csc x\) runs from \(-1\) down to \(-\infty\): every value \(\le -1\) is taken exactly once. So no horizontal line meets this piece twice (one-one), and every allowed value is reached (onto).
It is the same interval \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) that we used for \(\sin^{-1} x\), with only 0 removed (because \(\sin 0 = 0\)). This choice is what makes \(\csc^{-1} x = \sin^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\) true (Example 4 in 9.1.6).
The domain of \(\csc^{-1} x = \mathbb{R} - (-1, 1)\) and range of \(\csc^{-1} x = \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, 0\right) \cup \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).

The graph of the function \(\csc : \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, 0\right) \cup \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) \(\to (-\infty, -1) \cup (1, \infty)\) is shown in Figure 9.11(a) and graph of \(\csc^{-1} : (-\infty, -1) \cup (1, \infty)\) \(\to: \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, 0\right) \cup \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) is shown in Figure 9.11(b).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
In this sentence the book writes \((-\infty, -1) \cup (1, \infty)\) twice, with round brackets. The end points \(-1\) and \(1\) belong to the set, so the brackets must be closed: \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\). There is also a stray colon in \(\to:\), which should be just \(\to\). Correctly:
\[\csc^{-1} : (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\]
\[\to \left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right) \cup \left(0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\]

blocks.alt: Principal branch of y = csc x: for x in (0, pi over 2] the curve comes down from plus infinity near the y-axis to the end point (pi over 2, 1); for x in [minus pi over 2, 0) it starts at the end point (minus pi over 2, minus 1) and goes down to minus infinity near the y-axis. Dashed vertical lines at x = minus pi over 2 and x = pi over 2.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.11(a): graph of \(y = \csc x\) on \([-\frac{\pi}{2}, 0) \cup (0, \frac{\pi}{2}]\) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: The book's caption under Figure 9.11(a) reads 'Graph of \(y = \csc x\) from \(-2\pi\) to \(2\pi\)', copied from Figure 9.10. Figure 9.11(a) shows only the principal branch on \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, 0\right) \cup \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\); our caption says this.

blocks.alt: Graph of y = inverse cosecant of x. For x at least 1 the curve starts at (1, pi over 2) and decreases towards the x-axis without touching it. For x at most minus 1 the curve starts at (minus 1, minus pi over 2) and rises towards the x-axis without touching it. Dashed horizontal lines y = pi over 2 and y = minus pi over 2. Nothing is drawn for x between minus 1 and 1.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.11(b): graph of \(y = \csc^{-1} x\) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to read Figures 9.11(a) and 9.11(b) together: the graph of \(\csc^{-1} x\) is the mirror image of the principal branch of \(\csc x\) in the line \(y = x\). Every point \((a, b)\) becomes \((b, a)\):
\(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, 1\right) \to \left(1, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) and \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, -1\right) \to \left(-1, -\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).
The vertical asymptote \(x = 0\) of \(\csc x\) becomes the horizontal asymptote \(y = 0\) (the \(x\)-axis) of \(\csc^{-1} x\): as \(x\) grows large, \(\csc^{-1} x\) gets close to 0 but never reaches it, because \(\csc y\) is never infinite. That is why 0 is not in the range.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A quick example of our own. Find \(\csc^{-1} 2\) and \(\csc^{-1}(-\sqrt{2})\).
\(\csc^{-1} 2 = y\) means \(\csc y = 2\), i.e. \(\sin y = \frac{1}{2}\), with \(y\) in the principal range. So \(y = \frac{\pi}{6}\).
\(\csc^{-1}(-\sqrt{2}) = y\) means \(\sin y = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), so \(y = -\frac{\pi}{4}\) (not \(\frac{5\pi}{4}\), which is outside the range).
\(\csc^{-1}\frac{1}{2}\) does not exist: \(\frac{1}{2}\) is not in the domain \(\mathbb{R} - (-1, 1)\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\csc x\) has domain \(\mathbb{R} - \{n\pi\}\) and range \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\); it is periodic, so it is not one-one.
2. Principal cosecant function: \(\csc : \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, 0\right) \cup \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right] \to (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\).
3. \(y = \csc^{-1} x \iff x = \csc y\).
4. Domain of \(\csc^{-1} x\): \(\mathbb{R} - (-1, 1)\); range: \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, 0\right) \cup \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).
5. The two graphs are mirror images in \(y = x\); \(y = 0\) is a horizontal asymptote of \(\csc^{-1} x\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(\csc^{-1} x\) as \(\frac{1}{\csc x}\): the \(-1\) means inverse function, not reciprocal (\(\frac{1}{\csc x}\) is just \(\sin x\)).
2. Including 0 in the range: \(\csc y\) is undefined at \(y = 0\), so \(\csc^{-1} x \ne 0\) for every \(x\).
3. Giving an answer outside \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), e.g. \(\csc^{-1} 2 = \frac{5\pi}{6}\): true that \(\csc\frac{5\pi}{6} = 2\), but it is not the principal value.
4. Trying \(\csc^{-1}\) of a number between \(-1\) and \(1\): it does not exist.
